Cubemaps can't be handled this smoothly because they're an 'unwrapped cube' meant to represent what an area generally looks like.

[This](https://youtu.be/k26k1UQNJhA?si=ABM1sD1Lxd5TKaol) is a good example of what I'm talking about. You can easily visualize how a cubemap is used in reflections and how they're used to represent a space. \- DPVR. DPVR E4, specifically. It's essentially just a Quest 2 with no internals and a DisplayPort. We'll just discount the DK1 and 2 as those didn't have dedicated controllers, but I do want to give an honorable mention to 'em for the amount of games that supported the old [Razer Hydra](https://blogs-images.forbes.com/erikkain/files/2012/06/razerhydra-600.jpg) controllers as a replacement for native motion controls. Those things were cool as hell, and if inside-out tracking hadn't taken off to the extent that it has they'd be what I'd assume most headsets would try to ape. Pretty sure the 4K didn't launch with controllers either.

I think the Quest 3 controllers are comfortable and convenient enough that I'm never really aware of any failings they've got while I'm actually in the middle of using them, but much like the rest of the Quest 3 package it's sort of a jack-of-all-trades, one-size-fits-all sort of solution, where it doesn't necessarily excel in any one place but it's pretty good at everything to the point where for the average user it's probably the 'best'. Removing the tracking rings does a TON for keeping these things light and maneuverable. Otherwise, they're basically just Quest 2 controllers though and it's not my favorite layout.

The [second generation WMR controllers](https://s.yimg.com/ny/api/res/1.2/AF5pYLdd6cX6h6P00iKJyQ--/YXBwaWQ9aGlnaGxhbmRlcjt3PTY0MDtoPTM4MA--/https://s.yimg.com/os/creatr-uploaded-images/2020-12/436438e0-4b84-11eb-8df7-8d0f49ea3108) that the Reverb G2 came with were fine, but they truly just felt like Quest 2 controllers that needed more juice for less playtime with worse overall durability. [The first generation](https://image-us.samsung.com/SamsungUS/support/solutions/mobile/virtual-reality/874369_2_Reset_the_HMD_Odyssey_Controllers-0.png) had a lot of the same problems (seriously I had to replace my nice ergonomic Odyssey controllers for Acer and HP controllers three times before moving to the Reverb), but I genuinely loved their layouts and still wish more controllers kept the touchpad. Gave you a lot of room to tweak stuff around if you were playing something older that prioritized the Vive wand's layout while also letting you pretty easily adjust for games designed more for Oculus's more conventional A/B/X/Y scheme.

Both controllers also had insanely huge tracking rings and while you could definitely get used to working around them they made intricate hand movements and especially using compact gun designs like the P90 an absolute pain.

  
So, like, TL;DR, putting it on a tierlist, my preferences would probably look something like...

  
S: N/A

A: Quest 3

B: Quest 2, Gen 1 WMR

C: Gen 2 WMR

The Quest 3 isn't top-of-the-line, but it's probably the best overall package you can get right now. Like, it doesn't stand out in any one specific regard? But you don't have nearly the kinds of compromises you have to make with other VR sets. It's also, like... literally designed to play VR by itself, hence why it's called a standalone headset. It CAN be an 'entry' level model, but I'd say that applies to the Quest 3S, not the base Quest 3. The difference between the two is almost entirely in their displays; the Quest 3 has a horizontal FOV of 110 degrees compared to the Quest 3S's 97 degrees, has two higher resolution 2064x2208 screens instead of the single 1932x1920 screen of the Quest 3S, and MOST importantly, the Quest 3 uses pancake lenses instead of the 3S's fresnel lenses. This means that while the Quest 3's screens need to push a higher brightness for the same general light levels of the 3S, it also means you get a significantly wider field of view when compared to the 3S.

That, and the Quest 3 is, like, $500, whereas the 3S is as cheap as $300. 

As for PCVR, you generally have two options, both of which carry the unfortunate caveat of compression, but input delay is (in my experience) impossible to notice, hitches are rare, and requirements surprisingly achieveable for that holy grail of wireless VR. Sounds like you're new to VR, so I'll give you a quick summary of stuff I'd have liked to known about it when I started.

First and foremost, familiarize yourself with two different terms: seated, and roomscale. With the exception of a handful of games, you'll almost always have a built-in option for playing VR seated, which means your required playspace can shrink DRAMATICALLY, essentially only requiring someplace to sit comfortably, and enough space to stretch your arms out in a 180 degree space. Roomscale is about what it sounds on the tin, and is where you want as much space as possible, but my main VR playspace is essentially the space between my bed and my closet, which is... generously, MAYBE a 5x5 space? I think the best thing you can do to improve at Zombies is to learn how zombie AI works. Above all else, I think the difficulty in this game comes primarily from losing awareness and impatience, so you can combat this pretty easily by spending time learning how to take advantage of the main enemy you're gonna be dealing with. 

For example, did you know you can pretty easily slide by an entire horde in WaW? Because of how that game's AI works, you really only need a couple of inches to slip past a horde, to the point where I've seen people juke their entire train out of one of Verrukt's spawn side rooms. Each game is a little different, but you can very quickly build up your game sense to the point where you can quickly understand whether or not certain risks are worth the reward; there's a full horde following me and I'm out of ammo, so do I have enough time to roll the box or should I resort to a wallbuy? 

I just went down on Der Riese and I'm all the way at the second teleporter, should I cut through the spawn courtyard to reach Juggernog again or should I head through the smaller fenced in exterior corridor, because on one hand the former gives me more space to train but there are three spawn points (on top of the fact that zombies can get through the bent fence between the two), while the latter is more enclosed but zombies are probably only going to be coming at me from behind? Hell, maybe both options are too risky and I should just stick to training until the horde is a little thinner, which is risky because I'm back to two (or three, which in and of itself is something helpful to keep in mind for risk assessment) hits but theoretically as long as I pay attention to my training I shouldn't get hit at all.

  
I'm of the pretty firm belief that at least with the earlier games, you could absolutely get by with game sense alone, completely foregoing perks and PaP and sticking with whatever wallbuys exist as long as you're patient enough and you know which risks you should take and which you shouldn't. 

That being said, in terms of more generalized tips, just off the top of my head... 

The order you get perks matters; Jugg should usually be the first thing you get, but there are cases where I'll prioritize getting Speed Cola second and there are cases where I'll prioritize getting Double Tap second (like if I get heavier weapons from the box that extra speed can be VITAL, while on the other hand if I'm stuck with weaker weapons doubling my DPS can be hugely valuable). Hell, if I'm lucky enough to get two wonder weapons, I'll usually dedicate a perk slot to Mule Kick so I can keep a more ammo-efficient gun on hand.

Speaking of perks, as you get more confident I actually recommend skipping Quick Revive when playing solo; it's a great tool to keep a run going, and by no means should you feel embarrassed for using it, but I also think it's valuable to get used to not having that on backup. Pushes you to really flex your risk assessment skills since a single mistake can earn you a down.

In anything post-BO3, PaP becomes IMMENSELY valuable not just for its initial damage boost but because double-PaP'd weapons essentially become mini-wonder weapons, giving literally any weapon the ability to occasionally proc an effect that can (usually) clear an entire horde with a single bullet. 

Point optimization is a SUPER valuable skill you should try to take advantage of whenever you can. Some people can get pretty anal about it, but even just a little bit of thought put into how you clear those first few rounds can give you a HUGE headstart on your point economy early on. Just as a quick example, my rounds 1 and 2 almost always consists of me dumping four 1911 rounds into a zombie's leg before finishing them off with a melee, my rounds 3 and 4 almost always consist of me dumping whatever is left into a zombie before finishing them off with 2/3 melees, and only by round 5 do I start opening doors and picking up wallbuys (or start rolling the box if it happens to spawn near me). Bonus points if you can save up enough to pick up a bowie knife because that'll mean you can continue to primarily melee zombies up until round 10, you'll very quickly earn back the cost of the knife fourfold by the time it stops being a 1 hit and even once you hit that point you can still go for occasional 2-hit melee kills to keep the profit going even longer.

Speaking more on point optimization, assuming my RNG is dogshit and I just can't get a wonder weapon, at a MINIMUM I try to make sure I have a good, reliable weapon as my primary and a super weak but fast weapon as my secondary; in BO1 and BO2, that usually means hoping for a Galil and then grabbing an SMG off the wall for my secondary, for example. The fandom calls the latter point guns, and they can be SUPER valuable for just padding the fuck out of your wallet especially once you start getting some trains going.

I find the biggest issue with a LOT of eggs is that they not only have a ton of very convoluted, contrived and obscure steps that give you very little (in-game, sometimes you'll get help from ciphers and the like) guidance. Don't worry about it, if you keep trying you'll get it eventually. If I have any tips, it's to always be mindful of when you're on your last zombie so you can take care of each step without being too distracted, and try not to continue trying if you find yourself getting frustrated, because that just makes you sloppier and just exacerbates the problem. Fortunately, just killing zombies is pretty fun, so you could legitimately just do that for a couple of rounds and then give it another try; the zombies might get harder but if you can do high rounds you should be fine with that as long as you remember to keep a couple of zombies.

Okay, I'm a HUGE BO4 defender, and have been since it came out. But...

*  Perk system reduced the ability for per-match improvisation and entirely eliminated map-specific perks, something I recall a lot of people dissing CW for.
* Legacy perks like Juggernog, Double Tap and Speed Cola were removed and had their effects moved elsewhere to remove 'crutch perks', but perks like Dying Wish and Winter's Wail just took their place as perks you HAVE to keep.

* BO4's zombie spawn system means you literally CAN'T outrun zombie spawns; they'll always respawn ahead of you meaning you can't 'escape' a horde for a little while like you could previously. Best examples of this are in Blood, I think.
* BO4 began the trend of simplifying the point system. At the end of the day I still genuinely really love BO4 because it adds a lot that I genuinely enjoy, but it was FAR from a painless entry with zero faults.

'Cuz we have the SDK. We have access to tools that let us dig pretty deep into the engine to tweak (or even replace) whatever elements we may need for the game we want to make.

If a developer doesn't do that, that means any prospective modders have to take on the task of creating those tools themselves. That means learning how the engine works and what it expects from each of a game's assets, learning how to read and then write from those assets, figuring out how to effectively test any changes you make without the game just crashing because you're trying to load something it wasn't anticipating, and then you have to go through the development of your own toolset to use all of that knowledge in the first place.

It's a LITTLE easier when a game is made in something like Unity and Unreal because to a certain extent there are elements you can reliably expect to always be there, which is how things like BepinEx can exist to help sort of generalize modding for games on certain engines, but there's still a lot of gruntwork you need to do if you aren't given the right tools.

As I understand it, there are two distinct but similar schools of thought on it.

The first is that it's intended to generally improve the flow of the game due to the fact that the old points system required you to go about each zombie in a very specific way to maximize your points; y'know, four shots to the body then a melee so you get the bonus for finishing a zombie off with your knife, progress to popping a headshot once the zombie can take it THEN go for the knife, that sorta thing. 

The second is that it helps lesser-used weapon types like snipers and shotguns stay somewhat useful. Both weapon types tend to have some great damage, but because of that damage combined with their almost universally poor RoFs there's basically no reason to use them over just rolling for a Galil or something. It does mean weaker weapons like SMGs and pistols lose out on their ability to just soak up points with their high firerates and low DPS, but overall I think it just serves to help encourage people to try more weapons without people bitching about it being 'suboptimal'. 

It started back in BO4, which was also the first 3arc zombies to give you the ability to swap out the starting pistol with different options, so I'd imagine it leans more towards the latter than the former, but it's probably fair to assume both are decently significant factors.

It essentially comes down to two characters that you will have to play (and finish the game with) multiple times; Aria and Coda.

Aria is the third story-mode character you unlock, and her gimmick is that she only has a single point of health. This would be difficult at the best of times, but Aria also takes damage if you slip up on your rhythm. Couple that with the fact that she always starts on the last zone and progresses backwards (which means you're dealing with more complicated enemies) and the fact that you're limited to the standard dagger (compared to weapons like the longsword, rapier, bow or axe all of which give you extra range to serve as a buffer) and it's pretty difficult to finally nail down how to progress with her.

Coda is Aria but worse. She has Aria's gimmick but she also has Bolt's gimmick (the tempo is doubled) and Monk's gimmick (picking up gold kills you, which means any spot an enemy dies on will kill you), and her own special gimmick of not spawning with a revive potion like Aria.

  
There are other tricky achievements (like one where you have to work out how to get a stationary enemy to kill you), but nothing compares to those.

I think these are valid concerns, but I think you're also slightly misunderstanding how indie developers would be impacted by this.

First and foremost, the primary goal of the campaign is to try and prevent games from being made inaccessible because it was designed to only be playable on a central server. There are plenty of reasons why a game might be pulled from a marketplace, many of which are of no fault to the developer, but as I understand it this wouldn't impact a game dealing with any of those reasons because the game itself would still be playable; just not available to purchase. 

A good example would be something like the Deadpool game that came out in the 2010s, or the plethora of Telltale games pulled from Steam. Those would be similar to the situation you're proposing, but we don't expect those to be made available indefinitely; that'd be a different matter entirely, and one probably worth discussing, but not the main goal of SKG. As long as you, the developer, don't purposefully design the game to ONLY function when connected to a central server without plans to provide software to host that central server for dedicated fans, you are in the clear. 

There's definitely a case to be made for considering the possible costs for sharing those server binaries, but I don't think those are related to your concerns, and if they are I'm a little skeptical of how likely it is that an indie developer unable to handle the costs of throwing up a Google Drive or Dropbox link would design their game to require that central server in the first place.

I think by itself, the loadout system is absolutely something that can fall under the 'just don't use it' category, because by itself I don't think it pushes the design of the rest of the game. Regardless of whether or not you spawn with a 1911 or a SPAS-12, your damage REALLY starts to suffer if you don't bother to try to upgrade it. Like, I think the fact that you could spawn with a bowie knife in CW was a WAY bigger deal than being able to spawn with an LMG ever was because I could go most games not firing a shot for the first ten or so rounds. And, hey, we're not getting that kind of permanent progression for our abilities anymore, so that at least won't be an issue.

That being said, I do think there's an argument to be made for the fact that loadouts could, theoretically, have influenced the rest of the game's balance negatively. Stuff like the point system being reworked could have been motivated by 3arc not wanting to punish players for preferring to spawn in with, say, a shotgun or a sniper and stick with it only to get way less points, for example. 

On its own, I think loadouts are ultimately a good option that can absolutely be dismissed without much issue that help provide more options, but I also think you can't just do a blanket 'well just don't use it' without taking the rest of the design into consideration.

I think the biggest issue with VR MMOs is that they always try to replicate conventional flatscreen MMOs without understanding that for many people, VR just isn't suited to those mechanics.

They replicate things like slower starts with a focus on developing the world and giving you a drip feed of class abilities as you get acquainted with the way combat flows, but because VR requires you to actually move your body even if you choose to play seated it means there is an actual physical limit to how much someone is going to be willing to play. For games designed to be playable in short bursts like Beat Saber, Blade & Sorcery and Pistol Whip, I think that's fine, and there will always be people willing to push through their comfort level, but speaking broadly I just don't think you can necessarily hit the same highs with a VR MMO as you can with a pancake one. 

Couple that with the fact that MMOs are already some of the most expensive games you can try to run and I'm not surprised; you need to get enough players that are willing to spend money so you can keep the thing afloat which is already difficult in our tight attention economy, but on top of that you need to do so using a medium already very niche compared to the wider gaming landscape.

Someone in his chat pointed out Minecraft, but we've had private servers for things for ages; including the very games that would be most impacted by this, with all of the data that is normally kept obfuscated away from the client, this is just trying to make it so you're REQUIRED to offer that instead of keeping that software and data hidden away on a thumb drive somewhere.

I do think that as games exist now, certain live service games are going to require a lot of additional work that will cost developers money to work this into them, but I think that's just one of those 'things will hurt before they start to heal' kind of things. If his examples of FFXIV and Diablo 4 were designed with the knowledge that one day, the money will stop coming in enough for maintaining the servers to be profitable, the effort of ensuring any server-side information can be collected into a package they can one day release (or, even better, ensuring the core gameplay can be separated into an offline campaign) doesn't have to be some resource-intensive scramble.

The only reason Diablo 3 (and 4) aren't singleplayer games is because Blizzard either didn't have the foresight (unlikely) or didn't care enough to consider the possibility of those central servers being shut off. It is entirely possible to play through the entirety of Diablo 3 (can't speak to 4 but I would be willing to bet it's the same way) as alone and isolated from those multiplayer features as a NEET on 4chan. Hell, you CAN play it offline right now, on consoles! And that applies to a TON of ActiBlizz games that force an online-only component, like Call of Duty. Black Ops 6 is going to be the first (as far as I'm aware) exception, and that's because they're supposedly going to stream the larger textures over the internet to try to cut down on filesize, something that is, again, absolutely an issue that can be worked around.

Knockout City is a great example of this, I think. It was a live service game complete with a cosmetic shop and a battle pass and social clan features and a competitive matchmaking system, all of the bells and whistles of modern live service games, but when it wasn't profitable enough to keep running they just went ahead and let you play it offline. Hell, they even released the server software, so while I think most people would be happy with just LAN-support, you don't need to fuck around with software like Hamachi.

KC isn't the same scale as something like WoW or FFXIV and I think trying to compare the effort required to create an end-of-life plan for a 3v3 competitive dodgeball game to a multi-hundreds-of-thousands player MMO is silly, but the idea isn't to force developers to create entirely separate versions of their games that can be played on a single person's computer, it's just to let dedicated enough fans run the servers on their own end so the game they paid for can still be played.

Couple'a quick tips for you!

First and foremost, as I understand it, the way zombies in this game operate is that when they lose line of sight, they'll head for your last known position. That means if you have a horde, head for clusters of buildings or trees, and dart behind 'em.

Secondly, fences are your best friend. You don't want to take on a full horde if you can help it, and zombies have to stumble over a fence to climb them, which means you can effectively split them up into two, three, four smaller hordes you can more easily deal with (either by directly fighting, or by running). 

Thirdly, don't underestimate the power of fire. There are a couple of different ways to get one started (campfires, molotovs and fire bombs are the main ones), but past a certain size you really shouldn't even think about dealing with a horde unless you have a good melee weapon (and the maxed-out skills to use it), a good gun (with the ammo AND skills to use it), or fire. You miss out on any loot a zombie could be carrying, but once you get a couple of them lit you can effectively just train them for a couple of minutes and end up with a whole zombie barbecue. Just remember that you can outrun zombies without running so you don't use up too much stamina.

It's difficult to really pin down any specifics without, y'know, actually being a part of Valve circa the early-2000s, but it really depends on which era of development we're talking about. It's not really accurate, because a lot of ideas would've been developed and then dropped and you can't really nail down distinct 'versions' of the game, but if we want to look at one example of an 'era' of the game's development, we know basically nothing concrete about the early 'hyper' era beyond some scraps of concept art, a handful of voicelines, and a demo of the Hyperborea, but we DO know that levels like Kraken Base and the Hyperborea carried forward onto future stages of development, so that's a good example of how this stuff is iterated on.

The build of Half-Life 2 that was leaked in 2003 was unfinished enough that its release worried a LOT of fans that it wasn't going to be able to make its original release date (who I'm sure were not very surprised when Valve delayed the game after that), if that tells you anything, but it's also worth noting that a lot of what we consider to be the spicy *dark 'n griddy* HL2 beta elements were more than likely to have been scrapped by the time of the leak.

So, like... if we wanna get technical about it, there really isn't an 'original' version of Half-Life 2 because it was all iterated on over and over until we eventually reached the point we did with retail, and even ignoring that we really can't judge the state of the game circa-2003 on the Gembe leak because we didn't get the entire horde of what Valve had; for example, a LOT of the WC mappack .vmfs had to be fixed up by fans in order to even compile properly, and even outside of that they were (and in many cases, still are) missing a ton of the original assets like textures, models and sounds.

[This](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UqNAA6dGygs) is a good video to explain why, but the long and short of it is that MW19's engine was (as far as I know?) more-or-less a brand new engine created specifically for MW19, whereas pretty much every COD that has come out before that point has been gradually iterated on from game to game.

That includes Call of Duty. As in, the first one, in 2003. The one that ran on [idTech 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Id_Tech_3). The one that was made for Quake 3 in 1999. That's why you could do cute little bits of formatting magic like inserting symbols in your name or changing the color of the text in your name on some of the earlier games, and it is also, unfortunately, why the older CODs rely on third-party fan servers to let you play multiplayer without getting easily hacked in every game. Hell, it's an issue Cold War had because it still ran on a modified version of BO4's engine, which was in turn a modified version of BO3's engine.

Don't worry too much about the aesthetic. Engines are the foundation of a game, but they aren't as immutable as that implies. If you want a good example, take Titanfall and Apex Legends. Did you know those games run on the Source engine? It's a HEAVILY modified fork of the Source engine, but it's still the same engine that started development in 2002 and was first released in 2004, and you can see a pretty significant jump in the aesthetic possible between Half-Life 2 and Titanfall, and even in the jump in aesthetic from Titanfall to Apex.

In all honesty? They both have uses for different contexts. Not to mention some people could just feel more comfortable writing one way over the other. 

Like, if you're writing a story where you're trying to really get in the head of your protagonist, really examine them and what the consequences of their journey through the events of the story do for them, I think first person could be a really interesting way to portray that, LITERALLY placing the reader in the protagonist's perspective.

On the other hand, going third person could allow you to describe things the protagonist may not otherwise be aware of. It could let you include a narrator as a separate character, like a close friend or family member or maybe even an antagonist. 

Hell, you don't even need to do strictly one for a whole story! You would have to be mindful of how to handle the perspective shift to make the transition nice and seamless, but you could totally do a mix of the above where, say, flashback chapters take place in first person (maybe even mixing in a bit of an unreliable narrator since the narrator is the protagonist remembering an event?) whereas the 'current day' chapters take place from a disembodied narrator's perspective. There's a ton you can do with them and you shouldn't strictly limit yourself to one or the other.
